> @omarbenhamid thanks! I also have a couple of questions.
> 
> 1. Is there a reason to remove `authentication_classes` when initialising views as tools? DRF requests don't have a user set until the `_authenticate` method is called against `authentication_classes`, which messes a bit with logic that might depend on that. Do you mind if I add a switch in settings to actually use `DJANGO_MCP_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES` when doing `view_class.as_view`?
> 2. I would also like to include some django_request posprocessing as a part of _DRFRequestWrapper, for passing some custom params into the request. Do you mind if I add as a part of this PR?

I took a liberty of adding these toggles and post processing hooks support in the PR, if you don't mind, as only with those enabled our server would behave correctly. We're basically making a request on behalf of a user, so all permission and auth classes need to behave the same as they do for a regular API. I think that's a valid use case?

@omarbenhamid Addressed comments regarding permission_classes and docs. 
Hooks - cannot be addressed with a decorator or a middleware, since the library is effectively throwing away everything that might be added to request by using  _DRFRequestWrapper class. I also (and this is my personal opinion) really dislike the concept of signals, since you have much less control over the order in which they are executed. Hooks, as suggested in this PR, are simple and visibly tell you in which order they are executed.

Authentication - explained quite extensively. Because of the "bootstrap" call of another view inside the main API call, all the request data and context that is added to the main `/mcp` endpoint call is disregarded when `dispatch` is called on the wrapped view

Authentication - explained quite extensively. Because of the "bootstrap" call of another view inside the main API call, all the request data and context that is added to the main `/mcp` endpoint call is disregarded when `dispatch` is called on the wrapped view

I have been testing locally in our project with the updated library - with and without the authentication classes preserved, and if authentication_classes are omitted, the wrapped DRF view is always getting `AnonymousUser` when it tries to access `request.user`.

I guess the problem is that DRF view classes were not designed to be chain-called by other views, so all authentication and permission handling is internalised in the view class. To get around this you'd have to change how the wrapped view is called, potentially modifying either the `dispatch` method or rewriting a whole lot of DRF internal request handling with a mixin - but that seems more complicated right now compared to allowing the wrapped view to use internal auth mechanism one more time.

For the longer discussion 
I fully understand the limitations related to integrating DRF authentication. Currently Django MCP Server was not specifically designed for DRF but uses DRF Auth Classes as a handy way to support authentication without re-inventing the wheel. It turns out that this does not work well with DRF views. But I feel the option proposed of adding new settings and hooks ... is like a workaround of a more fundamental problem that we should solve, maybe just improving the request wrapper or devising a way to `request.user` after DRF dispatch() is invoked can solve your specific problem, may be not. What I would suggest would be : 

1. Revert back to 2205dbb and just from there update the documentation of the drf_ decorators and README. I can update the doc and README if you don't want to bother doing it.
2. Open an issue to deeply discuss the problems with the current DRF auth support and find solutions, hopefully by respecting better the DRF workflows rather than creating hooks and setting flags to work around it.

Great work, @Artui!

Just what I was looking for. It would be nice if, in the future, we could use the existing DRF Authentication already implemented on the API directly. This would save a lot of time reorganising the permissions and authentication.


Something like this:

```python
@drf_publish_viewset_mcp_tool
class SomeViewSet(viewsets.ViewSet):
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]
    authentication_classes = [JWTAuthentication]
```

>     permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]
>     authentication_classes = [JWTAuthentication]
> ```

Thanks! So permissions are going to be fixed in this PR. As for authentication_classes... I kinda understand now where the original idea for the auth classes being removed from the views comes from. 

Essentially - when you're publishing a view as a tool, it's not the published view that does authentication anymore, it's the main `/mcp` endpoint. 

So request goes 
`/mcp endpoint -> authentication using DJANGO_MCP_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES -> view invocation`
instead of 
`/mcp endpoint -> view invocation -> authentication based on the view class auth classes`

The main reason here being that the main endpoint not only handles tool calls, but also returns a list of tools, resources and prompts, all of which need to be secured behind an auth class.

If we were to delegate the authentication part to each specific tool, we would need either expose the entire `/mcp` endpoint as a public one (which might be a security concern), or dump all possible authentication classes from the published tools into DJANGO_MCP_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES, or sort of make that setting into a dynamic thing? Some part of the existing issue is fixed in [another PR](https://github.com/omarbenhamid/django-mcp-server/pull/27) though. The good thing though - you can populate DJANGO_MCP_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES with all possible auth classes in your app, and as soon as one of those works - you're good.

Hope this makes sense :D
